author: van de Schoot et al.
scope: Active-learning ASReview framework for transparent title/abstract prioritization
result: Open-source semi-automated screening system, with human-in-the-loop prioritization rather than a net person-time experiment
ref: Human-in-the-loop prioritization precedes LLM work; the present audit tests the interpretability of reported benefits, not tool design.

author: Chai et al.
scope: Research Screener simulations, interactive cases and sensitivity analyses
result: Reports workload reductions of 60--96% and a 12.53-day interactive time-saving comparison; task and calculation boundary matter
ref: Do not replace source-specific stage-level savings with an assumed total human team benefit.

author: Carey et al.
scope: Abstrackr-assisted screening in lymphoma review, N=7,723
result: 67% reported stage-1 workload saving (5.4 days), 91% sensitivity; 9% of stage-1 positives missed but none of these were final full-text inclusions
ref: An explicit example where title/abstract misses and final-inclusion misses are distinct outcomes.

author: Feng et al.
scope: 86 studies identified; 17 meta-analyzed for AI literature-screening performance
result: Maximized-recall and maximized-precision configurations have pooled recall 0.928 and 0.708, respectively (different optimization targets)
ref: Precision-recall optimization trade-offs were quantified years before this audit; not our novelty.

author: Ferdinands et al.
result: WSS@95 63.9--91.7%; introduced Average Time to Discovery, based on simulated screening order
ref: Time-to-discovery is a ranking/record metric, not observed net person-minutes.

author: Waffenschmidt et al.
scope: 11 searches and 33 selection processes with prioritization/single screening
result: Compared Rayyan/EPPI Reviewer prioritization at prespecified 25%, 50%, and 75% cutoffs
ref: Cutoff choice and comparator workflow must accompany any workload claim.

author: Chappell et al.
result: Explicitly discusses lack of comparative evidence for full review resource use and decision impact
ref: Source-to-claim audit operationalizes a pre-existing call for full-workflow evaluation.

author: Toth et al.
result: 89/123 concerned record screening; adoption/reporting heterogeneity noted
ref: A field map, not a directly comparable benchmark for PICOS or Mortensen.

author: Issaiy et al.
scope: 1,198 radiology abstracts, ChatGPT versus general physicians
result: Reported 95% sensitivity and 99% NPV; the model completed screening within one hour, physicians in 7--10 days
ref: Machine completion time and calendar days of another group do not identify matched net labor.

author: Scotti et al.
scope: 2,271 Cochrane, Campbell and Environmental Evidence reviews (2017--2024)
result: About 5% explicitly reported ML use; ML-enabled tool use often failed to disclose whether ML function was used
ref: Tool availability, declared usage, realized screening and timed benefits are separate claims.

author: Nordmann and Fischer
scope: ChatGPT structured inclusion criteria and mixed decision rules
result: Broad criteria favored sensitivity; narrow criteria favored specificity; conflict routing influenced workload
ref: Criteria formulation is part of the evaluation intervention; not measured downstream net staff time.

author: Harasgama et al.
result: 137/222 (61.7%) concerned title/abstract screening; landscape mapping rather than source-specific audit of causal labor
ref: Broad mapping already exists; our 54 inspected reports cannot be called a comprehensive survey.

author: Sung et al.
scope: 25 Cochrane reviews, general LLM and ASReviewLab ranking
result: A tail risk persists: for GPT-5, ranking down to the lowest-ranked supplemental included study would require passing 96% of abstracts
ref: Recall at a high-priority cutoff differs from retention of the last known included item; not human minutes.

author: Babaei et al.
scope: 4,482 citations in one scoping review, GPT-3.5 versus human labels
result: All 9 known final studies were recovered, but only 12/50 human title/abstract Includes overlapped AI (24% sensitivity versus human-screening reference)
ref: Two correct source statistics can use distinct references and cannot imply complete true recall.

author: T. J. Adam et al.
scope: 515 prompts, 4 medical review benchmarks, 12,360 pipeline runs
result: Average recall 83.6%, precision 18.5%; published work has a corrigendum (DOI 10.1017/rsm.2026.10104)
ref: Prompt selection and benchmark choice induce variation; estimates of time/cost are hypothetical and not our experiments.
